title: Closures: Fn, FnMut, FnOnce
summary: What a closure captures - and how - decides how many times you may call it.
lecture: A closure captures its environment as weakly as possible: reading a variable borrows it (&T), mutating borrows mutably (&mut T), and moving it out - or the `move` keyword - takes ownership. You don't declare this; the body decides.

The capture mode determines the trait: Fn (shared borrow - call it forever), FnMut (mutable borrow - call it repeatedly, needs a mut binding), FnOnce (consumes a capture - one call, then it's spent; a second call is E0382 on the closure itself).

The hierarchy nests: every Fn is FnMut is FnOnce. So a bound of Fn accepts the most closures for callers that call many times, and FnOnce is the most permissive to receive when you'll call exactly once.

Watch the Copy trap: `move` on an i32 moves a COPY - the closure gets its own counter, and the original never changes. Compiles fine, does the wrong thing; tests catch what the type system waves through.

example.caption: The body decides the capture; the capture decides the trait.
